claims.text: The initial material is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating bonded to a conventional metal substrate.
The initial coating has a moderate grain size and a conventional microstructure.
Increasing sliding speed increases frictional heat input.
At approximately 500 °C, increased sliding speed and frictional heating induce dynamic recrystallization in the coating near-surface.
The elevated-speed sliding condition induces near-surface nano-twinning.
Dynamic recrystallization and nano-twinning form an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The resulting grain refinement increases resistance to dislocation motion.
The refined microstructure acts as an internal barrier to shear deformation.
The microstructural refinement lowers the effective shear strength at the sliding interface.
Increasing sliding speed at approximately 500 °C lowers the coating wear rate relative to moderate-speed testing.
Increasing sliding speed at approximately 500 °C reduces microscopic plastic deformation relative to moderate-speed testing.
The prediction applies only when frictional heating is sufficient to trigger dynamic microstructural evolution.
The prediction ceases to apply when oxidation becomes the dominant wear influence.
The prediction ceases to apply if frictional heating causes phase instabilities.

contradictions.description: The grain-refined layer is said to increase resistance to dislocation motion and shear deformation, but it is also said to lower effective shear strength at the interface. These effects concern potentially different regions or definitions of shear strength, but that distinction is not supplied, leaving the stated mechanism internally inconsistent.
